name: Functional programming
summary: Build programs from functions that take values and return new values, without changing anything else along the way.
howItWorks: A pure function’s result depends only on its arguments, and calling it changes nothing outside it: no global variable, no field, no file. Data is immutable: to “change” an order you build a new order with one field different, and the old one stays valid for anyone still holding it. Functions are values too, so you pass them to other functions. `map`, `filter` and `reduce` take a function and replace most hand-written loops. A program becomes expressions that compute values rather than statements that update variables in order. Real programs still have to write to databases and send HTTP requests, so the usual design keeps those effects at the edges: a pure core makes the decisions, and a thin shell does the input and output. The pay-off is in testing and concurrency. A pure function is tested by passing inputs and checking the output, with no setup and no mocks. And because it touches nothing shared, calls can run in any order or on many cores at once. The costs are copying (new values instead of updates, which purpose-built persistent data structures make cheaper) and a style that takes getting used to.
analogy: A spreadsheet formula. `=B2*1.2` gives the same answer every time B2 holds the same number, it never edits another cell, and the sheet can recalculate cells in whatever order it likes.
useWhen: Transformations and rules: parsing, validation, pricing, reports, steps in a data pipeline
Logic you want to unit test without mocks or a database
Work you want to spread over many cores, or replay and get the same result
Rendering a UI from state, as React components and reducers do
avoidWhen: Hot loops over big mutable buffers (image processing, physics, numerics) where copying costs too much; mutate locally and keep the interface pure
Code that is almost all input and output, such as a script that moves files; plain steps read better
Chains of clever one-liners the rest of the team can’t read; name the intermediate steps
example: An online shop prices a cart with `total(cart)`, a pure function: the same cart always gives the same number, so its tests are a table of carts and expected totals, with no database in sight. The request handler is the only impure part: it loads the cart, calls `total`, and saves the result. Because `total` touches nothing shared, a nightly job can reprice 2 million carts by splitting them across 16 cores with no locks.

source: type Line = { readonly sku: string; readonly cents: number; readonly qty: number };
type Cart = { readonly lines: readonly Line[]; readonly coupon?: string };
// pure: the same cart in gives the same number out, and nothing else changes
cart.lines.map(l => l.cents * l.qty).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
// "changing" data means building a new value; the old cart stays as it was
const addLine = (cart: Cart, line: Line): Cart => ({ ...cart, lines: [...cart.lines, line] });
// higher-order: behaviour is passed in as a function
const linesWhere = (cart: Cart, keep: (l: Line) => boolean) => cart.lines.filter(keep);
const cart = addLine(addLine(empty, { sku: "mug", cents: 1200, qty: 2 }), { sku: "lamp", cents: 15000, qty: 1 });

sections.title: Functional style in mainstream languages
sections.intro: You don’t need Haskell to write this way. Most popular languages now ship the same building blocks.

rows.label: JavaScript, TypeScript
values: `items.filter(i => i.qty > 0).map(i => i.cents * i.qty).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)`
`map` and `filter` return new arrays and leave the original alone. Each step is eager and builds a full intermediate array.

rows.label: Java
values: Lambdas and streams arrived in Java 8 (2014). `parallelStream()` runs the same pipeline on many cores, and the docs warn that side effects in the lambdas break that.

rows.label: Rust
values: Iterators are lazy: nothing runs until something consumes them. They compile to roughly the same code as a hand-written loop.

rows.label: Python
values: `sum(l.cents * l.qty for l in cart if l.qty > 0)`
Comprehensions and generator expressions were borrowed from Haskell. Python code usually offers a pure interface but uses assignments inside.

rows.label: React
values: Components must be pure functions of props, state and context. Strict Mode calls each one twice in development to catch the ones that aren’t.

story: The idea is older than computers. In the early 1930s Alonzo Church developed the lambda calculus, a notation in which everything is a function applied to arguments; it later produced the first problem proved undecidable. In 1958 John McCarthy, building a language for artificial-intelligence work at MIT, wanted to pass functions as arguments (to apply one to every element of a list, the ancestor of `map`) and borrowed Church’s λ-notation to do it. The result was Lisp, implemented from the autumn of 1958 and described in his 1960 paper “Recursive Functions of Symbolic Expressions and Their Computation by Machine”. Lisp also introduced garbage collection, which frees programmers from tracking who still uses a value.

In his 1977 Turing Award lecture, John Backus, who had led the team that created Fortran, attacked the languages he had helped start. Programs written as assignment after assignment were, he said, “fat and weak”, tied to the “word-at-a-time” style of the von Neumann computer, with programming split into “a world of expressions and a world of statements”. He proposed a functional style built from combining forms, with an algebra for transforming programs. Meanwhile at Edinburgh, from 1973, Robin Milner’s group built ML as the scripting language of the LCF theorem prover, adding static types that the compiler inferred; it is the ancestor of Standard ML, OCaml and F#.

By the late 1980s there were many similar lazy, pure languages, and in 1987 researchers formed a committee to design a common one. The Haskell 1.0 report appeared on 1 April 1990. John Hughes’s “Why Functional Programming Matters” (1989) made the practical case: higher-order functions and lazy evaluation are new kinds of glue for building programs from small, reusable parts. Chris Okasaki’s 1996 thesis tackled a real cost, that most textbook data structures depend on assignment, with efficient purely functional ones. The ideas then went mainstream inside other languages: Java 8 added lambdas and streams in 2014, Rust made lazy iterators a core part of its standard library, and React made pure components its central rule.

choices.why: If a call can do nothing but compute its result, the order of evaluation stops mattering and a whole class of bugs disappears, as Hughes put it. Assignments are also what make programs hard to prove correct.
McCarthy needed to apply a function to every element of a list, so functions had to be arguments. That needed a notation for anonymous functions, and Church’s λ was the one to hand.
ML was the metalanguage of a theorem prover, so a well-typed program must not be able to produce a faulty proof. Milner’s inference gave that safety without making programmers write the types.
Delaying work until a result is needed lets programs be glued together from generators and consumers, even infinite ones. Hughes argued this is a key reason functional programs are modular.

timeline.text: Alonzo Church introduces the λ-notation for functions
McCarthy starts implementing Lisp at MIT
Milner’s group at Edinburgh begins LCF, whose metalanguage becomes ML
Backus’s Turing lecture: “Can Programming Be Liberated from the von Neumann Style?”
Okasaki’s thesis on purely functional data structures
